lesson.title: Interrupting in casual conversations (with friends and family)
head: Purpose
Phrase
Example
rows: *Wait, wait. You quit your job? When?*

**Sorry, quick question…**
**Can I just say something?**
*Sorry, quick question. Who else was there?*
*Oh, that reminds me, did you ever get your phone fixed?*
*Before I forget, your mum called this morning.*
*Anyway, where was I? Oh yes, the hotel.*
*Sorry, I keep interrupting. Go on, what did she say?*

lesson.title: Interrupting in professional settings (meetings, calls, presentations)
head: Purpose
Phrase
Example
rows: *Sorry to interrupt, but the client is waiting on line two.*
**Could I just ask a quick question?**
*Could I just ask a quick question about the budget?*
*Can I just jump in here? I think the deadline is too tight.*

lesson.title: When someone interrupts YOU
head: Purpose
Phrase
Example
rows: **If I could just finish (my point) first?**
*Good question, but if I could just finish my point first?*
**I'll come back to that in a moment.**
*That's a fair point. I'll come back to that in a moment.*
*As I was saying, the project should finish in June.*
*Oh, you wanted to say something? Please, go ahead.*
*Before we finish, does anyone have anything to add?*

items: When do you usually **interrupt people?** In what situations?

lesson.label: 📖 Bài học chính
lesson.title: 1. Casual: Wait, he did what?!
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Linh, Tom and Mai are having coffee. Linh is telling them about the blind date her aunt set up for her last weekend.*
lines: So, my aunt finally **set me up with** her colleague’s son. We met at a little Italian place on Saturday. He **turned up** twenty minutes late, and—
**Wait, wait.** Twenty minutes? Did he at least **apologise**?
**Sort of.** He **blamed** the traffic, but he didn’t seem that **bothered**. **Anyway**, we sat down and tried to **make small talk**.
**Sorry, quick question.** What does he do? Your aunt said he works in finance, right?
Yeah, at a bank. And that’s the thing. He **spent the first half hour** talking about his **investments** and his new car.
**Hang on a sec.** Half an hour? Did he ask you anything about yourself?
**Barely!** And whenever I tried to **change the subject**, he just gave me **one-word answers**. There were so many **awkward silences**. But wait, **I haven’t even got to the worst part yet.**
**Oh, that reminds me**, my cousin **went on** a date like that last month. The guy **kept checking his phone** the whole time!
Ha, that’s exactly what happened next! **Anyway, where was I?**

Oh, right. When the bill came, he said, “Shall we split it?” Which is totally fine! But then he took out his phone and **worked out** exactly what I’d eaten, **down to** the last slice of garlic bread.
No way! That’s **a bit of a red flag**. **Sorry, I keep interrupting. Go on!**
**No worries.** Honestly, we just **had nothing in common**, so I **called it a night** pretty early. My aunt keeps asking if I’ll **give him a second chance**. **I don’t think so!**

lesson.title: 2. Professional: In the meeting
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Mr Harris, the team manager, is explaining a new hybrid working plan at a team meeting. Laura and David are listening.*
lines: …so from next month, everyone will **work from home** on Mondays and Fridays and come into the office from Tuesday to Thursday. We'll run it as **a three-month trial**. During that time, I'd like—
**Sorry to interrupt**, but **could I just ask a quick question**?
Can we choose which days we work from home, or will those days be **fixed**?
Good question. Each team can decide, but everyone needs to be online and **available** between ten and four.
**Can I just jump in here?** I'm **a bit concerned about** team meetings. It's much harder to **brainstorm** on video calls.
**That's a fair point**, David. I'll come back to that in a moment. **If I could just finish** explaining the plan first?
Thanks. During the trial, I'd like everyone to **fill in** a short survey every two weeks to see **how things are going**. Now, **going back to** David's point about meetings…
Yeah. It's just much easier to **bounce ideas off each other** in person. On calls, it's harder to tell if everyone's **following the discussion.**
**Can I just add something to that?** Maybe we could **save the bigger meetings for office days**. Then home days could be for **getting individual tasks done.**
That's a great idea, Laura. It sounds like **a good compromise**. **Does that sound OK to everyone?**
Great. **Before we move on,** does anyone have anything else to add?
Just one thing. Will we be provided with any **equipment** for working from home, like a second screen?
I'm not sure yet. I'll **look into it** and **get back to you** by Friday.

homework.title: Part 1: Vocab check
homework.instructions: Fill in each blank with a phrase from the word bank. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Hannah has just started a new job. She meets her friend Sam for coffee.
lines: So, how's the new job going?
Pretty good! Yesterday, the team took me out for lunch so I could get to know everyone.
At first, it was a bit weird. Nobody really knew what to say, so we just tried to {make small talk} about the weather and the traffic. There were a few {awkward silences}.
Haha, that always happens at the start.
Then my manager started talking about work again, so I tried to {change the subject}. I asked everyone about their weekend plans, and that really helped.
Smart move. What's your manager like?
He's nice, but he seems quite {concerned about} deadlines. He kept checking his emails during lunch.
Not really. It's {hard to tell} after just one lunch. I'll wait and {see how things go}.
Fair enough. Do you get to work from home?
Two days a week. But honestly, I prefer the office. It's much easier to {bounce ideas off each other} when you're there {in person}.
Makes sense. So, are you going to the team dinner on Friday?
Probably, but I might {call it a night} early. I've got a busy weekend.

homework.title: Part 3A: Casual: a trip to Đà Lạt
homework.instructions: Complete the conversation with the phrases from the box. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Nam is telling his friends Lily and Hoa about his weekend trip to Đà Lạt.
bank: Sorry, I keep interrupting. Go on!
lines: So, on the second day, we rented motorbikes and drove up into the mountains. Then halfway up, it started raining really heavily, and…
{Wait, wait.} You drove in the rain? Weren't you scared?
A bit! Anyway, we stopped at a small café to wait.
{Sorry, quick question.} Who did you go with? Your colleagues?
No, my cousins. So, we were sitting in the café, and…
{Oh, that reminds me}, did you try the strawberry milk there? Everyone says it's amazing.
Ha, yes, I had three glasses! {Anyway, where was I?} Oh yes, the café. The owner told us about a secret waterfall nearby.
A secret waterfall? Wow! {Sorry, I keep interrupting. Go on!}
So, the next morning, we went to find it…

homework.title: Part 3B: Professional: a team meeting
homework.instructions: Complete the conversation with the phrases from the box. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Ms Chen is presenting the plan for the company's new website at a team meeting.
bank: I'll come back to that in a moment.
If I could just finish explaining the timeline first?

lines: …so the new website should be ready by the end of March. The design team will start next week, and…
{Sorry to interrupt, but} could I just ask a quick question?

Thanks. {As I was saying,} the design team will start next week, and we'll test the website in early March. Now, going back to Anna's idea about live chat…

homework.title: Part 4: Listening
homework.intro: Emma and Jack are colleagues. They're having lunch together after Emma's big presentation. Listen, then answer the questions.

script.text: So, how did it go? Was this your first time presenting to the CEO?
Yes, my first time. I was nervous, but I felt quite confident, because ==I practised it about ten times at home==. I knew every slide by heart.
Well, I started speaking, and everything was fine. But ==after about two minutes, my laptop suddenly went black==.
Wait, wait. Two minutes? That's so early!
I know! I tried to restart it, but it didn't work. In the end, ==someone from IT had to open my file on a different computer==. It took almost fifteen minutes.
Sorry, quick question. What did you do while you were waiting? Did the CEO take a break?
No, everyone just sat there, so ==I started talking without my slides. I told them a story about one of our customers== and why she loves our product.
Oh, that reminds me, ==my manager always says people remember stories, not numbers==. Nobody remembers a chart, but everyone remembers a good story.

That's exactly what happened! When the slides came back, I showed the sales numbers at the end. But afterwards, the CEO said the customer story was her favourite part. She said it was much more interesting than the numbers.
That's amazing! So, the laptop problem was actually a good thing.
Maybe! It went really well in the end. But ==next time, I'm going to bring a copy of my slides on a USB stick, just in case==.
Good idea. And maybe start with a story too!

questions.q: Why did Emma feel fairly confident before her presentation?
options: She had presented to the CEO before.
A colleague had checked her slides for her.
She had rehearsed it many times.
questions.why: “I felt quite confident, because I practised it about ten times at home.”

questions.q: Why is Jack surprised when Emma describes the problem?
options: It happened very early in the presentation.
It happened right before the end.
It happened before she had even started.
questions.why: “After about two minutes, my laptop suddenly went black.” Jack: “Two minutes? That's so early!”

questions.q: Why did it take so long to fix the problem?
options: Emma's laptop had to restart several times.
Someone had to open the file on another computer.
The CEO asked everyone to take a short break.
questions.why: “Someone from IT had to open my file on a different computer. It took almost fifteen minutes.”

questions.q: How did Emma deal with the wait?
options: She asked the CEO if they could take a break.
She started the presentation again from the beginning.
She carried on without her slides and told a customer story.
questions.why: “I started talking without my slides. I told them a story about one of our customers.”

questions.q: Why does Jack mention his manager?
options: To support the idea that stories are more memorable than data
To warn Emma that the CEO doesn't like long presentations
questions.why: “My manager always says people remember stories, not numbers.”

questions.q: What will Emma do differently next time?
options: Bring a backup copy of her slides
Ask IT to set up her laptop before she starts
questions.why: “Next time, I'm going to bring a copy of my slides on a USB stick, just in case.”

homework.title: Part 5: Speaking (1–2 minutes)
homework.instructions: Choose ONE of the three topics and record your answer (1–2 minutes).

options.title: Some people say interrupting shows you're interested. Others think it's rude. What do you think?
questions: Who interrupts the most in your family or group of friends?
When is it OK to interrupt, and when is it not?

options.title: Do you prefer working from home or in the office? Why?
questions: What do you like about working from home?
What's better about being in the office?
What would be a good compromise for you?

options.title: Tell me about the best or the worst meeting you've ever been in.
questions: What was the meeting about, and who was there?
What made it so good or so bad?
What did you learn from it?
